title: When Mice Got Cold, Their Goosebump Nerves Even Grew New Fur
hook: A study in mice found that the nerves and muscles that make goosebumps also control hair stem cells
summary: In mice, the nerve and muscle behind goosebumps also controlled hair stem cells. This study can't say whether the same is true in people.

text: When it's cold, the hair on your arm stands up and your skin gets bumpy.
In 2020, a Harvard team took a close look at mouse skin.
Everything in this story is a result from mice.
Goosebumps happen when sympathetic nerves squeeze the arrector pili muscle, the muscle that raises hair.
Under an electron microscope, those nerves turned out to connect to hair stem cells too.
When the muscle was removed, the link between the nerves and the stem cells broke.
When mice were kept in the cold for a long time, the nerves worked harder after the goosebumps appeared.
The stem cells woke up, and new hair started to grow in under two weeks.
However, this study can't tell us whether the same is true for people.

panels.text: It's a mouse result, so let's only believe that much!
